query: For MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials, what single intervention could improve mechanical performance while retaining a large magnetocaloric effect? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected changes relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a pulsed magnetic field treatment during post-solidification annealing of MnNiSi-based (Co,Ge‐substituted) magnetic refrigeration alloys will promote a more uniform dislocation arrangement and grain refinement, thereby enhancing mechanical strength and ductility while preserving the sharp magnetostructural transition that delivers the large magnetocaloric effect.
generation.material_initial_state: A MnNiSi‐based alloy that has been tuned via isostructural alloying (Co and Ge substitution) to lower its high structural transition temperature below the Curie point, thereby achieving a large magnetocaloric effect at room temperature but showing relatively weak mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Application of a pulsed magnetic field during the annealing stage of processing.
generation.conditions: Annealing the alloy at a temperature optimal for phase homogenization (approximately 400–500 K) while subjecting it to pulsed magnetic fields (e.g., pulse amplitude in the range of 1–2 Tesla with pulse durations/duty cycles similar to those used in studies on QAl9-4 aluminum bronze) under atmospheric or controlled inert gas conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain structure with a more uniform dislocation network and reduced residual stresses, induced by magnetic-field–assisted dislocation mobilization and rearrangement.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed magnetic field increases dislocation mobility and assists in depinning, which leads to a reorganization of defects and promotes grain refinement during annealing. This microstructural evolution enhances mechanical strength and ductility. Because the magnetostructural transition (the source of the large magnetocaloric effect) depends primarily on long-range magnetic ordering and unit-cell changes rather than on the detailed defect structure, the pulsed treatment is expected to improve mechanical attributes without disturbing the magnetocaloric function.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated alloys, the pulsed-magnetic-field–treated MnNiSi-based alloys will exhibit higher tensile strength and increased ductility while maintaining a magnetocaloric entropy change (ΔS) and refrigeration capacity close to the baseline values.
generation.baseline: MnNiSi-CoNiGe alloys processed without pulsed magnetic field intervention, which display the desired large magnetocaloric effect but suffer from irregular dislocation structures and larger grain sizes leading to lower mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The positive effect of the pulsed magnetic field treatment is anticipated only within a specific range of annealing temperatures and field amplitudes; excessive field strength or improperly chosen annealing conditions might perturb the delicate magnetostructural coupling, thereby diminishing the magnetocaloric performance.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about how a pulsed magnetic field will interact with the magnetostructural transformation in MnNiSi-based alloys. The hypothesis combines evidence from studies showing that pulsed magnetic field treatment improves mechanical properties in aluminum bronze (PMC10488801::web::015 and PMC10488801::web::023) with the established behavior of MnNiSi-CoNiGe systems in delivering large magnetocaloric effects (PMC4793218::web::000 and PMC4793218::web::011). The novel aspect is extending the pulsed magnetic field processing to MnNiSi-based alloys, a treatment that has not yet been explored in this system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MnNiSi-CoNiGe alloy samples. Subject one set to the pulsed magnetic field treatment during annealing (e.g., anneal at ~450 K under pulsed fields of ~1.5 T) while processing a control set without the magnetic field intervention. Conduct comparative mechanical tests and magnetocaloric characterizations on both sets.
measurements: Tensile tests to determine yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to evaluate grain size and dislocation structures.
Magnetization versus temperature and magnetic field measurements to assess the magnetostructural transition and calculate magnetic entropy change (ΔS) and refrigeration capacity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pulsed-field–treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in mechanical strength and ductility compared to controls, or if the magnetocaloric parameters (ΔS and refrigeration capacity) are noticeably reduced relative to the untreated baseline (beyond experimental error), then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: After magnetic field treatment, the alloy’s strength and plasticity increased simultaneously, while the alloy hardness decreased. That is mainly due to the increased dislocation density and grain refinement under a magnetic field, which improved the alloy strength. At the same time, the dislocation morphology changed from a disorderly arrangement to a locally ordered arrangement. Additionally, the number of dislocation entanglements decreased, and the dislocation distribution became more uniform, which is conducive to improving alloy plasticity. The mechanical properties and microstructure of the QAL9-4 aluminum bronze alloy for high-speed-rail brake calipers were changed by the pulsed magnetic field alone, which was mainly reflected as follows. (1) Under the influence of a magnetic field, dislocation becomes easier to depin and more mobile. At this point, LAGBs less than 2° move and splice to form subgrains or fine grains, thereby reducing the alloy’s average grain size. (2) After magnetic field treatment, the dislocation density of the aluminum bronze alloy increased, the distribution was more uniform, and the grain size and the residual stress decreased, which led to a synchronous improvement in the tensile strength and elongation of the alloy. (3) The strength and plasticity of the aluminum bronze alloy were improved by magnetic field treatment, and the nanosecond phase precipitated, which improved the wear resistance of the alloy.

The magnetostructural coupling between structural and magnetic transitions leads to magneto-multifunctionalities of phase-transition alloys. Due to the increasing demands of multifunctional applications, to search for the new materials with tunable magnetostructural transformations in a large operating temperature range is important. In this work, we demonstrate that by chemically alloying MnNiSi with CoNiGe, the structural transformation temperature of MnNiSi (1200 K) is remarkably decreased by almost 1000 K. A tunable magnetostructural transformation between the paramagnetic hexagonal and ferromagnetic orthorhombic phase over a wide temperature window from 425 to 125 K is realized in (MnNiSi)1−x(CoNiGe)x system. The magnetic-field-induced magnetostructural transformation is accompanied by the high-performance magnetocaloric effect, proving that MnNiSi-CoNiGe system is a promising candidate for magnetic cooling refrigerant.
